title: The Cities of Refuge
summary: The LORD tells Joshua to designate the cities of refuge that Moses had commanded, where a person who killed someone unintentionally could flee from the avenger of blood. The elders at the gate hear the fugitive's case, take him in, and protect him until he stands trial before the assembly and until the death of the high priest. Israel sets apart six cities, three west and three east of the Jordan, open to Israelites and foreigners alike.
story: With the land divided, Israel must now live in it justly. The first institutions set up in the settled land are not palaces or forts but places of protection for people caught in a tragedy. Moses had commanded these cities in Numbers 35 and Deuteronomy 19, and had already named the three eastern cities (Deuteronomy 4:41-43). This short chapter carries out that command in full. It sits between the tribal allotments of chapters 13-19 and the Levitical towns of chapter 21, and fittingly so: all six cities of refuge were also Levitical towns, placing the protection of life in the hands of those who served at God's sanctuary.
historical:
The six cities were spread through the whole land so that one was within reach of every Israelite. West of the Jordan, Kedesh lay in the hills of Naphtali in the north, Shechem in the hills of Ephraim in the center, and Hebron in the hills of Judah in the south. East of the Jordan, Bezer lay on the plateau in Reuben's territory in the south, Ramoth in Gilead in Gad's territory in the center, and Golan in Bashan in Manasseh's territory in the north. Several were already ancient and important: Shechem, where Abraham first built an altar in the land (Genesis 12:6-7), and Hebron, Abraham's home and Caleb's inheritance. Ramoth-gilead later became a contested border fortress where King Ahab died in battle (1 Kings 22).

The Old Testament doesn't record the cities of refuge being used in a specific case, though the principle of sanctuary appears when Adonijah and Joab grasp the horns of the altar (1 Kings 1:50; 2:28). Later Jewish tradition, gathered in the Mishnah (the collection of rabbinic law completed around AD 200), discussed the law of the cities of refuge in detail.
cultural:
In the ancient world, with no police force, justice for a killing was often the responsibility of the victim's family. The avenger of blood (goel) was the nearest male relative, whose duty was to pursue the killer. This system restrained crime but could also escalate into feuds and punish the innocent along with the guilty. The law of refuge limited it. It distinguished murder from accidental killing, which the law described with examples like an axe head flying off its handle (Deuteronomy 19:5), and it gave the accused a place of safety until a proper hearing could be held.

The city gate was where elders sat to hear cases and conduct business (compare Ruth 4:1-2). A fugitive stated his case there first, and the elders took him in. The assembly then judged whether the killing was intentional (Numbers 35:16-25). If it was murder, the refuge offered no protection. If it was accidental, the killer had to remain in the city until the high priest died, and only then return home. The law applied to "all the Israelites and foreigners among them" (verse 9), so the protection did not depend on belonging to Israel.
literary: The chapter is mostly divine speech. The LORD's instructions in verses 2-6 summarize the longer laws of Numbers 35 and Deuteronomy 19, moving in a clear sequence: the purpose of the cities, the fugitive's arrival at the gate, the protection from the avenger, and the conditions for return. Verses 7-8 report Israel's obedience in two balanced lists of three cities, each named with its region and tribe. Verse 9 closes with a summary that restates the purpose and extends it to foreigners. The chapter's key words, flee, refuge, avenger of blood, and unintentionally, are repeated so that its meaning is unmistakable.

outline.t: The LORD commands cities of refuge
How refuge works: the gate, the elders, the trial, the high priest
Six cities designated on both sides of the Jordan
Refuge for Israelites and foreigners alike

doctrines.note: The law distinguishes between murder and accidental killing, and it makes room for mercy without denying that a life has been lost. Justice in Israel was to be both serious about bloodshed and careful to protect the innocent.
Shed blood was understood to pollute the land where God dwelt (Numbers 35:33-34). The cities of refuge protected the land from both unpunished murder and the shedding of innocent blood in revenge.

The manslayer's release at the death of the high priest has been read by many interpreters as a kind of atonement: the death of the one who represented the people before God closed the matter. Others read it as an amnesty that marked the end of an era. Either way, a death brings freedom.

words.note: Miqlat, refuge or asylum. The word is used almost only for these cities. It describes a place received into, not a hiding place found by oneself: the fugitive had to be accepted by the elders and given a place to live among them.

Gaal, to redeem or avenge, used here in the phrase avenger of blood. The same word describes the kinsman-redeemer, like Boaz in Ruth, who bought back a relative's land or restored his family. Both roles belong to the nearest relative, who acts to set right what has been lost.

Shegagah, error or unintentional wrong. It is also the term for unintentional sins in the sacrificial laws of Leviticus 4. The distinction between intentional and unintentional wrongdoing runs through the whole Old Testament law.

Ratsach, to kill. This is the verb of the commandment You shall not murder (Exodus 20:13), yet here it is used even of accidental killing. The law takes every human death seriously, while judging the killer according to intent.

christ: The New Testament does not directly call Christ a city of refuge, but Hebrews uses the image of fleeing for refuge: it speaks of those who have fled to take hold of the hope set before them, a hope anchored where Jesus has entered as high priest (Hebrews 6:18-20). The comparison is thematic, and it has long been drawn by Christian readers. In both cases a person under threat flees to a place God has appointed, and in both cases release is tied to the death of a high priest. The difference is significant: the cities sheltered only the unintentional killer, while Christ, the high priest who died and lives forever, receives the guilty as well.
questions: Why do you think God's law distinguishes so carefully between intentional and accidental harm? Where do you need to make that distinction in how you judge others or yourself?
The cities of refuge were open to foreigners as well as Israelites. Who are the people in your community who most need a place of safety, and who might be overlooked?
What would it look like for a church to be a place of refuge, where people can be taken in, heard fairly, and protected while the truth comes out?
